reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / GOLD & ATS guidelines
clinicalPearls: Defined by permanent, abnormal dilatation of the bronchi, presenting with chronic productive cough, copious purulent sputum, and recurrent chest infections
Haemoptysis, breathlessness, and coarse crackles with occasional wheeze are common, and clubbing may be present in advanced disease
High-resolution CT is the diagnostic standard, showing airway dilatation greater than the accompanying vessel (signet-ring sign), lack of tapering, and airway wall thickening
Causes include prior severe infection, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, ABPA, and obstruction; a cause should be actively sought
Sputum microbiology guides therapy; chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation is associated with more frequent exacerbations and worse outcomes
Airway clearance techniques and pulmonary rehabilitation are cornerstones of long-term management
Exacerbations are treated with appropriately targeted antimicrobials guided by prior culture results, and long-term suppressive strategies are considered in frequent exacerbators
Assessment for treatable contributors such as immunoglobulin deficiency or ABPA can meaningfully change management
reference.pathophysiology: A vicious cycle of airway injury drives bronchiectasis: an initial insult (infection, impaired mucociliary clearance, immune deficiency, or obstruction) impairs clearance of secretions, allowing bacterial colonisation. Persistent bacterial presence provokes chronic neutrophilic inflammation with release of proteases and reactive oxygen species that progressively damage the bronchial wall, weakening and dilating the airways. The damaged, dilated airways clear secretions still less effectively, perpetuating infection and inflammation and leading to further structural destruction.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with chronic bronchitis
Pulmonary tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest to confirm and map the extent of airway dilatation
Sputum culture including for mycobacteria and fungi to guide targeted therapy
Immunoglobulin levels and other immune workup to detect underlying immunodeficiency
Testing for cystic fibrosis and, where suspected, ciliary function studies
Aspergillus-specific serology and total IgE to evaluate for ABPA
redFlags: Massive or recurrent haemoptysis requiring urgent intervention
Rapid clinical decline or systemic sepsis during an exacerbation
New isolation of resistant organisms or non-tuberculous mycobacteria
Progressive respiratory failure or features of cor pulmonale
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely with the underlying cause and disease extent; many patients remain stable for years with good airway clearance and infection control, but frequent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas colonisation, and extensive disease predict faster decline in lung function and higher mortality.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent chest infections symptomatically without imaging to establish the diagnosis
Failing to search for a reversible or treatable underlying cause
Neglecting airway clearance in favour of antibiotics alone
Not obtaining sputum cultures before escalating antimicrobial therapy
management: Establish daily airway clearance techniques and pulmonary rehabilitation as the cornerstone of long-term care
Treat exacerbations with prolonged, sputum-culture-guided antibiotics, and attempt eradication of newly isolated Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Offer long-term macrolide therapy such as azithromycin for frequent exacerbators, with nebulised antibiotics for chronic Pseudomonas colonisation

Identify and treat the underlying cause: immunoglobulin replacement for antibody deficiency, cystic fibrosis modulator therapy, or corticosteroids and antifungals for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Use mucoactive agents and nebulised saline, adding bronchodilators where airflow obstruction coexists
Give influenza and pneumococcal vaccination and support smoking cessation
Monitor with regular sputum microbiology and lung function, and manage significant haemoptysis with bronchial artery embolisation
Refer for surgical resection of localised disease or lung transplantation in end-stage disease
